The Economics of Going Electric in California, Gas to Grid

NEM 3.0 hasn’t broken the economic case for home electrification. But it hasn’t delivered the battery-storage incentive it may have been designed to create.

CLAIM 1

At current 2026 costs, batteries do not pencil out in the four NEM 3.0 case studies. The 2025 ITC changed that result in 2 cases

The full 8,760-hour co-optimization chooses no material battery capacity under current law in all four case-study counties (0 of 4 above 0.1 kWh). In the weighted 12×24 sensitivity, the lower 2025 ITC-adjusted capital cost produces more than 0.1 kWh in 2 of 4 cases, reaching 5.53–7.50 kWh. The sensitivity curves show the mechanism: as storage becomes cheaper, optimal storage and PV rise together.

0 of 4current-law exact 8,760-hour solves with more than 0.1 kWh of storage; maximum modeled capacity is 0.00 kWh
2 of 42025 ITC weighted 12×24 observations with more than 0.1 kWh of storage
$500–$1,200per kWh, the highest tested current-law 12×24 sensitivity-grid price still producing more than 0.1 kWh of storage
Cost scope used above: PV is held fixed within each policy panel—$2,310/kW with the 2025 ITC and $3,300/kW under current law. The displayed battery-capex sensitivity spans $25–$1,500/kWh and includes solved grid observations at both modeled market prices ($1,022.448/kWh and $1,460.64/kWh). The current-law diamond additionally reports the dedicated 8,760-hour solve.
Why this happens: the optimization model’s own logic. The result looks paradoxical only if solar and storage are substitutes. In the objective function they are complements, and the reason is two terms:
Objective: minimize annual cost ($/yr)
PV·cpv·αpv + B·cbatt·αbatt + ∑h wh·(grid→load)h·pimp,h − ∑h wh·(pv→grid)h·pexp,h + deg
  • capex annualized cost of the solar and battery you build.
  • pimp solar is paid the full retail price (averaging ~$0.480/kWh across the top 10% of modeled import-price hours) on every kWh it lets you not import.
  • pexp but only the lower ACC export credit (~$0.057/kWh when hourly prices are weighted by modeled PV generation) on what it sends to the grid.

A battery earns only the difference between those two prices, net of ~10% round-trip loss and a mid-life replacement. So the battery only enters when it is cheap. When it does, it can let surplus midday solar reach higher-valued hours instead of being exported immediately. Cheaper storage raises the optimal amount of solar in the modeled sweeps. It never replaces it.

One sentence for the skeptic: the battery is not a substitute for solar. It is what lets the marginal kWh of solar reach the peak price instead of the export price, which is exactly why optimal solar goes up, not down, as storage gets cheaper.
Robustness: what if installers oversize solar? In practice a system is often sized to offset 100% of annual consumption, not to the economic optimum. That larger array (here 7.3 kW, versus the ~2 kW optimum) spills far more midday surplus; the modeled PV-generation-weighted export credit is ~$0.057/kWh, so a battery has more to store. Does storage then pencil?

Checks tied to this claim

  • tests/lp_cooptimize_test.py checks that sizing uses the configured capital costs and the repository’s annualization primitives.
  • tests/solar_storage_dispatch_test.py checks hourly energy balance, state of charge, and physical meter direction.
  • tests/tariffs_source_test.py checks the source-locked import, NBT export, ACC Plus, and NBC tariff primitives.
  • figure_builder/tests/test_datasets.py checks exact market-point selection and complete source coverage; figure_builder/tests/test_recipes.py checks that captions are derived from current modeled values.

Capital-cost inputs, not market findings

  • Current law: PV is $3,300/kW and battery storage is $1,460.64/kWh net of modeled federal incentives.
  • 2025 ITC sensitivity: PV is $2,310/kW and battery storage is $1,022.448/kWh net of the 30% federal ITC.
  • These are declared model inputs. The figures test economics at those costs; a separate capital-cost benchmark review is needed before treating them as estimates of today’s market price.
